extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, reporters, media scholars, and general readers interested in journalistic ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards about what 'objectivity' in journalism means, critiques of that ideal, and alternative practices for reporting (e.g., fairness, transparency, peace journalism, crowdfunding safeguards). Useful for assessing news reporting and newsroom norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic objectivity (umbrella definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic objectivity may refer to fairness, disinterestedness, factuality, and nonpartisanship; it most often encompasses all of these qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectivity aims to help the audience make up their own mind by providing facts and letting audiences interpret them; it evolved as a professional norm and is the philosophical basis of major news agencies that avoid overt partiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: A commitment to reporting only accurate and truthful information, without skewing any facts or details to improve the story or better align an issue with any certain agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truthfulness requires verification and avoidance of deliberate distortion; it's identified as one of the three interrelated concepts that define objectivity (truthfulness, neutrality, detachment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutrality / Nonpartisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should be reported in an unbiased, even-handed, and impartial manner, with journalists siding with none of the parties involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutrality entails presenting relevant facts and information from all sides; historically adopted by wire services to reach diverse subscribers. Critics argue strict neutrality can obscure truth or favor powerful institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should approach issues in a dispassionate and emotionless attitude so stories can be presented rationally and calmly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detachment is meant to let audiences form their own judgments; critics argue excessive detachment can be 'heartless' or inappropriate for emotionally charged issues like war or human rights abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making judgments; attribute information
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists (especially wire agencies) traditionally avoid making judgments and instead attribute information to spokespeople, the press, or other sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice reduces reporter assertion and places facts on record via sources; it can lead to reduced responsibility in reporting and has been part of agencies' effort to provide a single objective feed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present facts regardless of personal beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should present the facts whether or not they agree with or personally endorse those facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective reporting aims to portray issues neutrally regardless of the writer's opinion; this is often phrased as reporting facts first and allowing audience interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance / Fair chance to respond
rubrics_metrics.description: Give all sides their respective points of view and allow other sides a fair chance to respond; balance fosters fairness even if the reporter takes a side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 'fairness and accuracy' standard, taking sides is permitted provided accuracy and opportunity to respond are observed; this is an accepted practical alternative to strict neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not create a 'false balance' by presenting victims and perpetrators as equivalent or by giving undue weight to fringe or harmful positions in the name of neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: detached accounts of lynchings that recounted alleged transgressions of victims normalized violence; editors should avoid false-equivalence framing that misleads audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: View from nowhere (critique of 'neutral' stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of adopting a neutral viewpoint 'from nobody's point of view' that can create the impression of authoritative impartiality and may disinform audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars argue the 'view from nowhere' hides interpretation and can gain undeserved trust; critics recommend transparency about perspective instead of pretending to be neutral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency (as alternative to hidden neutrality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be open about the journalist's perspective, methods, and limitations to legitimately earn audience trust rather than hiding behind the appearance of impartiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency is advocated by commentators like Jay Rosen as a way to replace the 'view from nowhere' and to allow journalists to defend their choices more honestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge biases and limits of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should acknowledge, humbly and publicly, that their work is subjective and that they do not know everything, rather than masking ignorance behind a façade of objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brent Cunningham suggests admitting subjectivity, encouraging expertise, and identifying assumptions to reduce the harm of concealed bias; practical for building trust and improving reporting quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop expertise and act as sensemakers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters are encouraged to develop deep subject-matter knowledge and use it to sort competing claims, explain assumptions, and make informed judgments about what audiences need to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expertise allows journalists to go beyond mere neutral summarizing and to provide context, analysis, and reasoned evaluation while still striving for accuracy and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy / journalism of attachment (alternative normative stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some argue journalists should overtly advocate for social justice or other causes, prioritizing advocacy above traditional objectivity constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proponents (e.g., Glasser) contend that putting social justice first may better serve the public good; critics counter that advocacy risks partisan reporting unless clearly labeled and accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peace journalism (conflict reporting alternative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply social-science-informed practices—conflict analysis, conflict resolution, peace research—to reporting on conflict instead of relying on conventional 'objective' practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peace journalism aims to introduce empirical insights that can replace unacknowledged conventions and provide more constructive coverage of wars and conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid speed-driven shallow reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that 24-hour news cycles and the prerogative for speed can push reporters toward convention-based or lazy reporting rather than principled truth-seeking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars note speed imposes pressures leading to event-driven coverage, pack behavior, reliance on existing narratives, and selection driven by news values—editors should mitigate these tendencies to preserve quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of conflict and sensationalism biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters are biased toward conflict because it is more interesting, which can distort coverage priorities and framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should counteract a bias toward conflict/sensationalism by valuing explanatory and contextual reporting and resisting incentives that favor conflict for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowdfunding safeguards to protect editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: When journalists use crowdfunding, adopt strategies to maintain objectivity/independence: construct an imaginary 'firewall' between funders and editorial decisions, limit investment from any single source, and clearly define the relationship with funders at the outset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study findings: passive investors typically don't interfere, active investors may provide feedback or early copies, and journalists feel accountability to funders; explicit safeguards help preserve editorial autonomy while using crowdfunding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize economic and institutional drivers of objectivity norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that objectivity as an industry standard arose partly from commercial pressures (attracting advertisers, seeking broad markets) and technological constraints (telegraph, speed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This historical and economic context explains why objectivity became normative but also why it may accommodate compromises (e.g., to avoid offending advertisers) that affect news selection and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fairness and accuracy as a pragmatic standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than strict neutrality, adopt fairness and accuracy: accurate reporting and giving other sides a fair opportunity to respond; allows responsible advocacy when justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups like Fairness and Accuracy in Reporting enshrine this approach; it provides a practical rubric for evaluating whether reporting is acceptable even when not strictly 'objective.'
